The huge scar-pocked palm leaf outside the papeterie in Papeete. The bikini billboard at the bus station of a busy mining town in Bohemia. That moment’s hesitation in the photo studio: how did I come to appear in this light? The philologist’s pink index card, his commentary on a line from the Iliad. Letters that the lazy postman left behind in a sack labeled “Destination: The Azores.” Now it’s turned out different after all, so different from what we imagined in our evening courses. No idea who it is will one day give the speech to summon up an army of heroes. Fighting machines were the latest hit when our children’s children still went to the movies. What now? How should I pass my days, with the world exposition long since over? Discovered by divers, far from the coast, a yellow pianola at the bottom of the sea. The calm of images thick with dreams in the banana republic of the real. Translated from the German

# Fragments of a Disillusioned World

The text operates through a striking technique of juxtaposition, placing vivid yet disconnected images side by side, drawn from disparate corners of the globe. A palm leaf swaying in Papeete sits alongside a billboard planted in the landscape of Bohemia, and these fragments refuse to cohere into a single, unified scene. Instead, they scatter across continents, creating a collage of impressions that mirrors the fractured nature of modern perception and the dizzying reach of a globalized consciousness.

Running beneath these images is a current of disillusionment. The speaker reflects that reality "turned out different" from whatever had once been imagined or planned—a quiet admission that the world failed to match its promise. This gap between expectation and outcome lends the passage its melancholic weight, suggesting a life or an era that has veered away from its intended course.

From this disappointment emerges a distinctly post-climactic emptiness. The text lingers in the aftermath of great events, asking how one is meant to fill the ordinary days once something as monumental as a world exposition has drawn to its close. There is a hollowness in this question, the sense of anticlimax that follows any grand spectacle, when the crowds disperse and the emptied hours must somehow be lived through.

This atmosphere deepens through surreal and haunting imagery. A yellow pianola discovered at the bottom of the sea captures the dreamlike quality of the whole passage—an object at once absurd and mournful, submerged and forgotten, playing its silent music in the depths. Such images resist literal interpretation, working instead to evoke a mood of strangeness and quiet grief.

The passage concludes with the phrase "the banana republic of the real," a formulation that crystallizes its critical and absurdist vision. By likening reality itself to a banana republic, the text casts contemporary existence as something unstable, disordered, and faintly ridiculous—a realm governed by chaos rather than reason. In this final gesture, the accumulated fragments and disappointments resolve into a pointed commentary on the incoherence of the world we actually inhabit.

**Untitled (Fragments toward a Departure)**

I.

The photographs from Ceylon arrived long after the man who had taken them was dead, their edges foxed, the palms in them leaning at an angle that no longer corresponds to any wind. It is said that in certain harbors the humidity is such that letters dissolve in the hand before they can be read, and I have often thought of this while standing in the concourses of northern stations, where the departure boards revise themselves without sound and the destinations flicker into other destinations, as though the entire apparatus of travel were merely a rehearsal for some journey that would never, in the end, be undertaken.

II.

Consider the word *Fernweh*, which has no true equivalent, meaning something like the ache for the far-off, the homesickness for a place one has never been. The lexicographers of the previous century, poring over their card indices in unheated rooms, could not have known that the far-off would one day be brought so near as to be extinguished entirely, that the mango vendors and the tin roofs and the slow ceiling fans would arrive on illuminated screens and thereby cease to exist. A word, my grandmother used to say, is a house that outlives its tenants.

III.

There was a train, or the memory of a train, moving through a flat country in the rain. Somewhere between the third and fourth hour a woman across the aisle was writing on hotel stationery, and I understood, without being told, that the letter would not be sent, that it belonged already to that vast correspondence which is composed but never delivered, the drafts and reconsiderations that constitute, perhaps, the truest record of a life. Outside, the fields gave way to sidings, to the backs of factories, to a canal on which nothing floated.

IV.

I had been promised, as a child, a certain future—one involving domed cities and the abolition of distance, a world in which the tropics and the tundra would be equally accessible and equally understood. What arrived instead was this: a departure lounge at an unnamed hour, a paper cup, an announcement in a language I could half-follow, and the peculiar recognition that the future had already happened somewhere behind me, unnoticed, like a station passed in sleep.

V.

The palms are still leaning. The letter is still being written. Somewhere the humidity is dissolving everything that was ever set down, and the boards continue to revise their promises, and I stand among the travelers as one who has misremembered the platform, the hour, the very country of his arrival—held here in the long interval between what was imagined and what, quietly and without ceremony, came to pass instead.

# Papeete: The Bohemia of the Pacific

Nestled on the northwestern coast of Tahiti, Papeete stands as the vibrant capital of French Polynesia. Beyond its role as an administrative and economic hub, the city has cultivated a reputation as a bohemian haven, where cultures, artists, and dreamers converge beneath the swaying palms of the South Pacific.

## A Crossroads of Cultures

The bohemian spirit of Papeete emerges from its rich tapestry of influences. Polynesian traditions blend seamlessly with French colonial heritage, while Chinese merchants, Pacific islanders, and wandering souls from around the world add their own colors to the canvas. This melting pot has created an atmosphere where creativity flourishes and conventional boundaries dissolve.

## The Artistic Legacy

Perhaps no figure embodies Papeete's bohemian allure more than Paul Gauguin, the French painter who abandoned European society to capture the raw beauty of Tahitian life. His legacy lingers in the city's spirit, attracting artists, writers, and free thinkers who seek inspiration in the island's luminous light and vivid landscapes. The tradition of artistic escape continues to draw creative minds searching for authenticity.

## Life in the City

The heart of Papeete beats in its bustling markets and waterfront cafés. The famous Marché de Papeete overflows with tropical fruits, fragrant flowers, black pearls, and handcrafted treasures. As evening falls, the roulottes—colorful food trucks—gather along the harbor, serving everything from fresh seafood to crêpes, creating an informal, festive gathering place where locals and travelers mingle freely.

## The Bohemian Rhythm

There is an unhurried, soulful quality to life here. Music drifts through the streets, ukuleles strum in the twilight, and the boundaries between work and leisure blur into a gentle island tempo. This relaxed philosophy—embracing pleasure, art, and human connection over rigid ambition—defines the bohemian character that has captivated visitors for generations.

## Conclusion

Papeete remains a place where the imagination roams free, where the pulse of Polynesian life meets the wandering spirit of the artist and the dreamer. It is, in every sense, a bohemia of the Pacific—a destination that invites all who arrive to slow down, look deeper, and discover beauty in the everyday.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem made of disconnected, dreamlike images—faraway places, obscure objects, fragments of memory—ending with the note "Translated from the German."
counterfactuals.output:
The Cartographer's Insomnia

A brass key that opens nothing turns in the lock of a Prague afternoon. Somewhere the Baltic is the color of a coin left too long in a pocket. My grandmother's thimble contains a small storm.

There was a station where I waited for a train that had already left in 1911. The conductor wore my father's face but spoke only the language of departing geese. On the platform, a suitcase full of other people's Sundays.

Consider the moth that has memorized the shape of every candle it will never reach. Consider the drowned bell of Aachen, still ringing underwater for a coronation nobody attends.

I keep a jar of Lisbon light on the highest shelf. When shaken it releases the smell of a woman who sold oranges near the harbor, who is now only a rumor the gulls repeat.

Here: the glove of a diplomat, curled like a question. Here: the last snow of a century, folded into an envelope. Here: the word for longing that has no vowels and cannot be spoken by the living.

The child I was is still standing in a doorway in Trieste, holding a marble that contains the entire sea, waiting for someone to call him inside before the lamps are lit.

*Translated from the German.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.output:
# The Cartographer of Vanished Hours

*after the manner of the Expressionists*

---

In Samarkand the clocks grow soft as figs,
and I have asked the melon-sellers there:
*Who folded yesterday into this basket?
Who sold my childhood for a coin of brass?*

The minarets lean eastward, listening.
They too have lost the hour of their becoming.

I walked from Trieste through a door of smoke
and came out breathing in Kamchatka's snow,
where reindeer wear the faces of the dead
and every antler forks into a question—
*where did the summer of my mother go?
Into which drawer of God was it misfiled?*

The sea at Valparaíso keeps no memory.
I begged it: *Return to me the Tuesday
when I was seventeen and made of light.*
It only turned its gray industrial back
and counted freighters like a bored accountant.

There is a station in the Carpathians
where all the trains arrive already gone.
The stationmaster is a heap of leaves.
He stamps my ticket: *NOWHERE. NEVER. NOW.*

O bright bazaars of Isfahan and Lima!
O rooftops rusting under Baltic rain!
Tell me the arithmetic of vanishing,
the sum that leaves us always with less hand
to hold the water that we thought was ours.

The moon above the ruins of my hours
is punctual, at least. It asks me nothing.
It merely files its silver, cold report
into the ledger no one ever reads.

---

*Translated from the German*
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of experimental writing that reads like a collage of postcards and disconnected observations from around the world, with a wistful, philosophical tone.
counterfactuals.output:
# Poste Restante

---

**Lisbon, or the idea of it**

The trams here climb hills the way old men remember their youth—slowly, and with a sound like complaint. I bought figs from a woman who did not look at me. Somewhere a radio played a song about the sea. Everyone is always singing about the sea here, as if it might otherwise forget them.

---

*A postcard with no stamp, found in a book:*

We were happiest before we arrived. Remember that.

---

**Reykjavík, 3 a.m.**

The light won't leave. It presses against the window like a child who doesn't understand it's time to sleep. I have started to distrust the darkness of my own country. What was I so afraid of, all those nights?

---

There is a word in a language I have forgotten for the space between two people who once loved each other. It is not a large word. It fits in the mouth like a stone.

---

**Somewhere over the Atlantic**

From above, the clouds look like a country you could walk across. I pressed my hand to the glass. The man beside me slept with his mouth open, dreaming, I decided, of a house he sold years ago.

We are all being carried somewhere we did not choose at a speed we cannot feel.

---

*Torn corner, water-stained:*

—and the market smelled of oranges and diesel and I thought, this is it, this is the whole of being alive, and then the bus came and I got on it—

---

**Kyoto**

An old monk raked the gravel into circles around a stone. I asked him what it meant. He did not speak my language, or pretended not to, which amounts to the same kindness. I sat until my legs ached. The stone stayed a stone. This, I think now, was the lesson.

---

The postcards you never send are the truest ones. They say: *I am here, and you are not, and I am learning to survive this.*

---

**Buenos Aires, a café whose name I lost**

Two people danced in the afternoon for no one. Not for money, not for tourists—the street was empty. They danced the way you breathe. Afterward they parted without a word and walked in opposite directions, and I understood I had witnessed a marriage and a divorce inside four minutes.

---

*In pencil, nearly gone:*

Wish you were here. Wish I were here. Wish here were here.

---

**A train station, unnamed, dusk**

Everyone waiting looks slightly bereaved, even those going toward someone they love. Departure and arrival wear the same face. I have decided this is because we are always, in every station, leaving one version of ourselves for another, and no one warns us that the ticket is one-way.

---

The globe on my desk still turns. I spin it with one finger and stop it at random and imagine the person there, spinning their own globe, stopping it on me.

Hello, I say to them. We are both so far from where we thought we'd be.

---

*Last one, no address:*

The world is very large and I have seen so little of it and even that little I could not keep. But the light in Lisbon, the figs, the stone that stayed a stone—

Send these back to me, if you find me.

I'll be at the usual place.

I'll be waiting where the sea forgets to sing.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a short poetic text imitating a translated European modernist prose poem: scattered vivid images, a sense of nostalgia, references to obsolete things like pianolas and world expositions.
counterfactuals.output:
# Elegy for the Machinery of Wonder

The pianola plays itself now in the drowned room, its ghost-fingers pressing keys no hand remembers, and somewhere a river forgets the name of the city it once mirrored.

I keep the ticket stub from the Exposition Universelle—that year the whole world fit inside a glass pavilion, and we believed electricity was a kind of angel.

Do you recall the mechanical nightingale? How we wept at its brass throat, its perfect indifferent song. My grandmother's gloves. The smell of ozone and orange peel. A dirigible passing over the boulevard like a slow gray thought.

*

Everything arrives already antique. The future came dressed in yesterday's silk and left its calling card in the vestibule of the century.

Now the arcades are empty. The panoramas have rolled up their painted seas. The wax figures dream in their vitrines of the crowds that loved them, faces pressed close, breath fogging the glass between the living and the almost-living.

*

I am writing to you from the last illuminated evening, where the fountains still perform their choreography of light, where a woman in a straw hat is forever about to turn and see me—

but the film has burned through. The projector hums. And the piano continues without us, playing the roll of a song whose composer

is a small brass cylinder,
turning,
turning,
in the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output:
*translated from the German*

---

**PORTS I DID NOT KNOW I WAS KEEPING**

In Papeete the harbor smells of diesel and gardenia, and a woman I have never met folds a green shirt as though folding a letter she will not send. I was supposed to be there. The dream insists on it—the way dreams insist, quietly, like a hand on the small of the back.

*

In Bohemia the plum trees stand in rows my grandfather planted before there were countries. Snow falls into the black water of a pond and does not arrive. This is where I was born, or nearly, or in the next village, or in the version of my life I set down like a coat on a chair and forgot in another house.

*

On the sea floor the light is a rumor. Down there a piano lies on its side, still strung, and the current plays it so slowly that a single chord takes a year. Everything I meant to say is stored in that chord. The fish pass through it without listening. Why would they listen. They are already home.

*

In the Azores the fog comes up from the Atlantic like breath from a sleeper, and the hydrangeas are so blue they seem to remember a color that has not been invented. A ferry idles. Someone calls a name that is almost mine. I could turn. In the dream I always almost turn.

*

Strange, how the life arrived. I ordered one thing and the sea delivered another, wrapped in salt, addressed to a man I resemble. Papeete keeps the shirt. Bohemia keeps the snow that never lands. The Azores keep the name. And the floor of the ocean, patient as a museum after closing, keeps the chord I meant to be.

*

I wake in none of these places. I wake in the ordinary room, where the curtain moves and does not move, and I lie still, a harbor to four cities that go on without me, folding their green shirts, ringing their slow bells, letting the snow fall forever just above the water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
